text: IT asset management practice. Same physical items configuration management just taught you about -- tracked for a completely different reason.

ITIL 4's purpose statement here is heavily financial and legal: plan and manage the full lifecycle of all IT assets to maximize value, control costs, manage risks, support decisions about reuse and retirement, and meet regulatory and contractual requirements. Notice the vocabulary -- cost, risk, regulatory, contractual. That's the tell that this is really a business practice wearing an IT hat, more than a purely technical one.

An asset's story starts before it's even unboxed. Planning: deciding what to buy and why. Procurement: the purchase order, the vendor, the cost. Deployment: who has it and under what assignment. Operation: is it still under warranty, is its license still valid. And eventually retirement -- decommissioning, data wiping, and disposal, which can itself carry regulatory weight if the asset ever touched regulated data. This practice owns visibility across that entire arc.

Here's the distinction worth sitting with. A configuration item is tracked because it plays a role in delivering a service. An asset is tracked because it has financial, contractual, or lifecycle value -- purchase date, warranty, license terms, depreciation. One laptop can be both at once: a CI because an employee's work depends on it, and an asset because the organization paid for it and needs to track its license and depreciation schedule. Same object, two separate reasons to care.

Software license compliance is a textbook example. Whether you're running more copies of an application than you're licensed for has nothing to do with how that app relates to other CIs -- it's a contractual question about entitlement versus actual usage. Audits and true-up fees live squarely in asset management's territory, because they're about the terms under which the asset was acquired.

Good asset data is what lets an organization reuse a laptop instead of buying a new one, retire hardware before its warranty window closes, and prove license compliance before a vendor audit forces the issue. Next, we turn from managing what exists to deliberately getting better: the continual improvement practice.
